title: PaperCut: One Small Breach, a Much Larger Footprint
summary: PaperCut put a card skimmer on about 80 newspaper websites through one shared payment form. How to check for it before Black Friday, and why blocking beats detection.
body_markdown:
*PaperCut is the latest in a fast-growing string of software supply chain attacks on websites and apps. Heading into Cyber Week, the danger isn't one deep wound. It's death by a thousand paper cuts.*


**The short version:** PaperCut put a card skimmer on about 80 newspaper websites through one shared payment form, and nobody noticed for six days. Security teams can check for it, and close the gap it used, before Black Friday. It's also the latest cut in a fast-growing string of software supply chain attacks, after OPTIMJACK, the Polymarket compromises, the AppsFlyer SDK and the PHP2Shell and Node2Shell flaws, with AI helping attackers find the next one faster. Entering Cyber Week, the pace is the problem, and the answer is blocking unauthorized code before it reaches a customer, for security and for PCI DSS.


## PaperCut: one line, 80 checkouts, six days


From November 13 to 19, about 80 US newspapers, including the Boston Herald, the Denver Post and the New York Daily News, served a card skimmer to readers buying subscriptions.[Guardio Labs found](https://guard.io/labs/papercut---80-us-newspaper-websites-served-a-credit-card-stealer) that someone had added one line to the card form those papers share, a form hosted by the payment processor Payway inside a subscription checkout built on Naviga's software. That line loaded a small file disguised as an old jQuery release from a public code CDN. The file connected to the attacker's server, which sent back the skimmer. When a reader hovered over the pay button, it took the card number, expiry date and security code, plus name, email, phone and address.


The newspapers' own pages never changed, and none of their defenses flinched. The skimmer lived inside the processor's trusted frame, sent stolen data over WebRTC instead of a normal web request, and was handed fresh to each visitor so scanners never found it in a file. Guardio counted more than 100,000 loads of the malicious file before the line came out after their report.


## Check for the cut before Black Friday


PaperCut is fixed at the source, but the gap it used is still open on most checkouts. Before the weekend, security and payments teams can:


- **Look for this exact cut.** Search hosted payment forms and checkout templates for the loader path Guardio published (cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/fs82g9omml) and check for traffic to 89.116.171\[.\]109 and 89.117.134\[.\]66. Organizations that took card payments through an affected form between November 13 and 19 should talk to counsel about card-breach notification.
- **Treat the processor's form as part of the checkout.** List every hosted payment form and embedded frame on payment pages, and ask each provider what changed in their form this month and who can edit it.
- **Watch for connections that aren't web requests.** A payment page that opens a WebRTC connection to an unknown server is a red flag that Content Security Policy won't catch.
- **Lock down the payment page.** Make sure only authorized scripts can run on checkout, and block the rest, rather than waiting for an alert after the fact.


## Not one cut. A thousand.


On its own, PaperCut is a small cut. Look at the rest of the year and a pattern appears: attackers are going after the software supply chain again and again, because one compromised vendor reaches everyone who trusts it.


Two weeks ago,[OPTIMJACK](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/optimjack-supply-chain-attack/) planted a card skimmer in a trusted testing script that ran on 178 organizations' websites for about 16 hours.[Polymarket was hit twice](https://www.feroot.com/blog/lessons-from-the-polymarket-breach/) this year through third-party code that drained users' wallets.[AppsFlyer's JavaScript SDK was compromised](https://www.feroot.com/blog/appsflyers-javascript-sdk-has-been-compromised/) to push malicious code to every site that loaded it. And AI-assisted research turned up server flaws like[PHP2Shell](https://www.feroot.com/blog/php2shell-cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/) and[Node2Shell](https://www.feroot.com/blog/node2shell-cve-2026-111497/) , which in the worst case let an attacker run code on a web server, and a compromised server can push malicious scripts to every visitor.


Most of these came through a vendor, a script, a form or an SDK that someone had already approved, and none of those needed the victims to make a mistake. That's how a thousand paper cuts work: no single one looks fatal, and together they bleed a business dry.


## Why Cyber Week makes every cut deeper


The cuts are coming faster. Days ago, the Director of National Intelligence[warned](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/22/jay-clayton-tech-outages-faa-microsoft-thanksgiving.html) that AI is helping attackers strike at a scale nobody has seen, and most of the industry's AI defense is busy in the server room. The client side, the code running in shoppers' browsers and mobile apps, is still guarded mostly by allowlists and periodic reviews that trust the source instead of checking what the code does.


Now add Black Friday and Cyber Monday: the heaviest checkout traffic of the year, change freezes in place, and teams stretched thin. A cut that runs for six days in mid-November reaches thousands of readers. The same cut over Cyber Week reaches far more shoppers, with far less time to respond.


## A bandage can't keep up


Detection is a bandage. It shows where the bleeding is, usually after a card brand or a researcher points it out. At this pace, a team that only detects will spend Cyber Week applying bandages. Blocking stops the blade before it touches skin: an unauthorized script that tries to read the card field simply doesn't run.


PCI DSS 4.0.1 points the same way.[Requirement 6.4.3](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/document_library/) asks organizations to authorize every script on payment pages, justify it and confirm its integrity. Requirement 11.6.1 asks for a way to detect unauthorized changes and raise an alert. The clearest proof that only authorized scripts run is a control that stops the rest and keeps a record. And as PaperCut shows, the company whose checkout the customer used carries the scar, even when the bad line lived in a vendor's form.


## Stopping the bleeding for good


A one-time check catches yesterday's cut. Staying ahead of a thousand takes a control that runs all the time. Feroot's AI-powered platform maps every script, tag-manager addition, hosted form and frame on login and payment pages, plus the SDKs inside mobile apps.[DXSecure](https://www.feroot.com/dxsecure/) learns how each script normally behaves and flags the instant one starts reading card fields or sending data somewhere new.[PaymentGuard](https://www.feroot.com/pci-paymentguard/) enforces which scripts can run on payment pages, blocks the ones that shouldn't, and keeps the evidence a QSA will ask for under Requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1. MobileGuard extends the same visibility to apps.


## Scratch or scar


Without blocking, the next supply chain cut lands on Black Friday, runs through Cyber Monday and surfaces weeks later in a card brand's notice. With it, the script reaches for the card field and never runs. The team gets an alert and a clean audit trail, and shoppers never feel a thing. Attackers are using AI to find the thinnest edge on every checkout. The teams that come through the season unscarred will answer with AI that watches every script and blocks the ones that don't belong.
